name: Kate
catalog_quote: The first syllable of a word always carries the heaviest stress (indicated by ´), and weaker stresses (`) occur on the alternate following syllables. In three syllable words, however, the weak stress on the third syllable is often omitted. Examples are: há.ta 'road', ká.ro.rac 'cloud' and sá.ma.rì.e.kac 'he exerted himself'.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is present verbatim (modulo scanned spacing) in the held PL-C41 scan at p. xx under 'Stress Placement', with the pp. xxi-xxii continuation also matching. (2) The classification 'fixed-strict', rule 10/100/1010/10100... (initial primary, alternating secondaries, optional loss of the third-syllable secondary in trisyllables) is exactly what McElhanon states, including his remark that diphthongs count as single vowels for stress. The source is a professional linguist's phonological sketch (1976/77) by the leading Huon-languages specialist, and it is the same source StressTyp2 and Gordon 2002 rely on. (3) Against Glottolog's bibliography there is no reference grammar, phonology monograph or instrumental study of Kâte; the two plausible modern candidates (McElhanon 1974 Kivung; Suter 2018 thesis) were fetched sources and are silent on stress placement.
